replying_to: Replying to MIKE - Multi-task Implicit Knowledge Embeddings by Autoencoding through a Shared Input Space
display_title: Official Review of Paper4411 by Reviewer 4jro

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors introduce a novel method for learning an encoder producing image embeddings from a series of source models (or teacher models), a method which they call MIKE (Multi-task Implicit Knowledge Embeddings). The encoder is obtained by training an auto-encoder to reconstruct an image. The original input and its reconstructed version by the auto-encoder pass through the source models and the loss is computed as the difference between the activations of the original input and the reconstructed version through the source models. The core intuition is that a reconstruction that preserves the patterns which are salient to the source network should produce activations that are similar to those of the original data.
The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the method on a preliminary small-scale setup.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The method seems novel and simple.
- The intuition and motivation are well explained.

Weaknesses:
- Though the preliminary results are encouraging, the paper is half-baked and requires more experiments to demonstrate the claims and analysis to understand the method.
- Results are sparse, preliminary and the broadness of the setup doesn’t allow to draw general conclusions.

Questions:
- I don’t get what the “baseline” (blue) and the “single task” (orange) setups are in Figure 3. What are their respective averages?
- What does “trained against” mean?
- How are the 3 tasks chosen in Figure 4?
- What’s the main takeaway of Figures 5 and 6?
- Experiments only consider segmentation source models (i.e. same tasks but on different domains or targets). Could you elaborate on how the method would work (and how well) if you consider source models with different tasks (image recognition for instance)?
content.summary_of_the_review:
The results of this paper are preliminary and the paper is half-baked.
I would suggest resubmitting to the next relevant conference when the paper is ready.

content.title: Response to Review 4 (4jro)
content.comment:
> I don’t get what the “baseline” (blue) and the “single task” (orange) setups are in Figure 3. What are their respective averages?

The first paragraph of section 4.2 attempts to explain the experiment which produced the results shown in Figure 3. The baseline (blue) is an autoencoder trained through pixel-wise reconstruction loss using the same data as the experimental (orange) network. Both of these autoencoders have the same topology; the only difference is how their training loss is generated. The experimental (orange) autoencoder is trained to absorb the knowledge from a single-task segmenter instead of using pixel-wise loss. Our setup is admittedly complex and could benefit from further explanation with the aid of additional figures.

> What does “trained against” mean?

When an autoencoder is “trained against” a given source network, said autoencoder is being trained to absorb the implicit knowledge of said source network using the loss defined in Equation 1.

> How are the 3 tasks chosen in Figure 4?

Admittedly, these 3 tasks were chosen arbitrarily. We plan to introduce a more diverse set of tasks and try absorbing the knowledge of the respective task experts (i.e. source networks) in various combinations.

> What’s the main takeaway of Figures 5 and 6?

Figure 5 shows stable convergence when the loss is applied to all layers of the source network with equal weight. Figure 6 shows that convergence becomes unstable when the loss weight is moved through the layers sequentially. In particular, the significant increase in error when moving to the later layers suggests a weak/unstable gradient from those layers.

> Experiments only consider segmentation source models (i.e. same tasks but on different domains or targets). Could you elaborate on how the method would work (and how well) if you consider source models with different tasks (image recognition for instance)?

We plan to introduce more diverse tasks in our follow-up experiments. Regardless of the tasks they were trained on, our method works best when all source networks have the same input shape. However, there are techniques for absorbing knowledge from source networks that differ in their input shape. These techniques will be discussed in the next iteration of our paper.

> The results of this paper are preliminary and the paper is half-baked. I would suggest resubmitting to the next relevant conference when the paper is ready.

We agree and plan to do so. Your feedback is appreciated.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4411 by Reviewer tXme

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for representation learning where embedding spaces from many different models can be merged into a single shared embedding space. Given a collection of source networks with different embedding spaces, the method involves training an autoencoder using two losses: (1) the reconstruction loss, and (2) loss from difference between source networks’ representations for the original input and the corresponding reconstructed instance. To evaluate the proposed method, experiments are conducted on the image segmentation task from COCO for 11 different task category sets, using EfficientNet based models, and evaluated using IOU.
content.main_review:
The idea presented could be interesting for scenarios that involve distilling representations from multiple networks into one, eg. for models from many different domains, different tasks etc. The approach, which is an extension of prior work from Larsen et al., (2016); Hou et al., (2017) to the use of multiple networks from which to distill, is clearly presented. However, the paper takes only a small step in validating the idea and doesn’t quite conduct extensive enough experimentation to make a convincing argument in favor of it. 

Some questions that might be useful to consider, especially for evaluating the quality of the learned representations (this is a very small subset):
1. How does this approach compare to simply training/fine-tuning a multi-task model? Establish the trade-off between using this process vs. just gaining access to some data. This is even more important when considering pre-trained models.
2. How does combining representations from truly different tasks impact performance? In the current study, the task remains image segmentation. What about representations from networks trained on image classification, object detection etc.? 
3. What about vastly different domains -- radiology images + imagenet + street scenes etc.? Why not just jointly train on these domains rather than distilling?
3. Even within segmentation, consider experiments using multiple datasets for more robust conclusions.

It’s not clear what the baseline in Figure 3 is, but it seems to be comparing the single-task version? Is it presented as analysis for why the general approach is useful? 

In addition to further experiments, it might be worth revising the narrative to make it clearer with stronger motivations and perhaps motivating examples as well -- what is a scenario where the source network and query data are available but no training data at all? 

Overall, the ideas presented could be interesting but the experiments are far too preliminary.
content.summary_of_the_review: Recommending rejection because experiments are unconvincing and preliminary.

content.title: Response to Review 3 (tXme)
content.comment:
> How does this approach compare to simply training/fine-tuning a multi-task model? Establish the trade-off between using this process vs. just gaining access to some data. This is even more important when considering pre-trained models.

Thanks for the suggestion. We will design our subsequent experiments to provide this as one of the baselines.

> How does combining representations from truly different tasks impact performance? In the current study, the task remains image segmentation. What about representations from networks trained on image classification, object detection etc.?... What about vastly different domains -- radiology images + imagenet + street scenes etc.? Why not just jointly train on these domains rather than distilling?

To address this, we plan to look at diverse tasks in the autonomous vehicle domain, including depth-estimation (i.e. pseudo-lidar), pedestrian detection, sign classification, and segmentation (ex. drivable space, signs, sky).

> It’s not clear what the baseline in Figure 3 is, but it seems to be comparing the single-task version?...

Each of the 11 radar charts in Figure 3 are indeed comparisons for the single-task version of each of the 11 COCO segmentation tasks. The baseline autoencoders use the same topology as the experimental ones and are trained using the same dataset. The only difference is that the baseline is trained directly from the dataset using pixel-wise reconstruction loss, while the experimental model is trained on the dataset indirectly by absorb the knowledge of a segmenter that was pretrained on the same dataset. To explain this more clearly, we will consider creating additional figures.

> In addition to further experiments, it might be worth revising the narrative to make it clearer with stronger motivations and perhaps motivating examples as well -- what is a scenario where the source network and query data are available but no training data at all?

Thanks for the suggestion. There are potentially many good example scenarios involving embodied agents. Robots (such as autonomous vehicles) often process far more data than can be feasibly stored, with many newer learning techniques able to train on this serial data-stream without catastrophic interference. However, a more current scenario might be one where you have obtained a collection of networks for which the training data is unknown, such as proprietary networks, and wish to consolidate their latent knowledge into a smaller network.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces MIKE, a Multi-task Implicit Knowledge Embedding model, to transfer knowledge from pre-trained networks to a single autoencoder.  Both the pre-trained networks and the autoencoder are based on EfficientNet. MIKE  considers that the inputs of the pre-trained networks and the autoencoder must be identical. The input X is passed through the autoencoder to return a reconstruction X’. Then both X and X’ are fed to the pre-trained networks to produce two sets of activations taken from all the hidden layers within the pre-trained networks. The loss function is based on the difference between these two sets. After training, the encoder of the autoencoder can be reused for downstream tasks.
content.main_review:
Pros. 

N/A

Cons. 

+ The paper is not well-structured, and it is hard to follow, e.g., using different terms (e.g., source, teacher, segmenter) to refer to the same concept (e.g., pre-trained).

+ The paper lacks the motivations. Why does MIKE need multiple pre-trained networks? Why doesn’t MIKE utilize a single network pre-trained on 11 different datasets? 

+ It’s is not really true when considering non-overlapping classes as different tasks. Why does MIKE use the loss function in Equation 1?

+ The baseline model is the single autoencoder which is not a good baseline. MIKE is incremental from the model proposed in [1] and does not compare with this model.

[1] Deep Feature Consistent Variational Autoencoder. WACV 2017.

content.title: Response to Review 2 (wgZg)
content.comment:
> The paper lacks the motivations. Why does MIKE need multiple pre-trained networks? Why doesn’t MIKE utilize a single network pre-trained on 11 different datasets?... It’s is not really true when considering non-overlapping classes as different tasks… The paper lacks the motivations and is not well-structured.

We need to better articulate our motivation earlier in the paper. Use-cases for MIKE would be situations where you have access to a large set of unwieldy pre-trained networks, but don’t have access to the datasets that were used to train them (thus preventing training of a single network on all datasets). The goal would be to consolidate the implicit knowledge of these networks into a much smaller network which can produce embeddings that make the absorbed knowledge accessible for downstream tasks. You are correct in pointing out that our preliminary experiments did not demonstrate this type of use-case, but instead aimed to determine basic feasibility of this method of knowledge transfer. We plan to withdrawal the submission until we are able to complete further experiments which actually demonstrate the stated purpose of MIKE.

> Why does MIKE use the loss function in Equation 1?

The loss function in Equation 1 forces the autoencoder to extract the patterns from data which caused the specific intermediate activations in the source/teacher network, thus absorbing the implicit knowledge/features represented in said intermediate activations. However, our use of mean-squared-error in Equation 1 was admittedly an arbitrary decision. Other distance metrics may in-fact be better suited to our purpose (we are open to suggestions).

> The baseline model is the single autoencoder which is not a good baseline.

The baseline model is the exact same autoencoder topology as the experimental model it is compared to, with the only difference being the loss equation used in training (simple pixel-wise reconstruction error for the baseline). It is unclear what would serve as a better baseline.

> MIKE is incremental from the model proposed in [1] and does not compare with this model.

The topological details of the models used in our preliminary experiments are of limited significance since we are trying to develop MIKE as a more general technique. Granted, the analysis of learned representations in [1] is something we would like to replicate for the sake of comparison.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work aims to learn a shared embedding space in an auto-encoder architecture (student network) which potentially encodes the knowledge from various source (teacher) networks. These teacher networks are trained on the same/similar datasets for different tasks.
The  auto-encoder is optimized such that the reconstruction from the auto-encoder has same activations in the source networks as the original input. For this a weighted loss function which minimizes the layerwise mse loss between the activations of the original input and the activations from the reconstructed input. 
Thus the work claims to induce knowledge embeddings where the loss (eq. 1) is aggregated for different source networks. 
The method is constrained in the sense that the input formats of the student network is identical to that of the teacher networks.
Experiments are performed on subsets based on objects of the COCO datasets for the segmentation network where the training stability and number of source networks from which knowledge can be transferred.
content.main_review:
Novelty: The novelty in terms of architecture and the task explored remain limited as there exist work eg., [a] which also aim to learn a shared feature space in an autoencoder in the multi-task setup. The related work should also be cited and compared to. 

Experiments: 
1. The choice of the architecture for the auto-encoder is not clear. How are the number of layers for encoder/decoder chosen? Also, if the reconstruction is nearly perfect owing to the number of parameters in auto-encoder, how does this impact the learning (gradients/parameter updates) of the auto-encoder network and the shared embedding space?
2. The experimental setup for multitask learning through knowledge distillation has been demonstrated in prior work [a,1] and the experimental setup consider in the paper is very different from the related work. 
3. The claims of scalability of the approach and the quality of the embeddings learnt by the method is not demonstrated in the experiments. 
4. There are issues regarding the training instability when considering deeper source networks. This should be discussed in more detail. This can potentially be resolved with the proper weighting of the loss functions?

content.title: Response to Review 1 (fuGi)
content.comment:
> The novelty in terms of architecture and the task explored remain limited as there exist work eg., [a] which also aim to learn a shared feature space in an autoencoder in the multi-task setup… The experimental setup for multitask learning through knowledge distillation has been demonstrated in prior work [a,1] and the experimental setup consider in the paper is very different from the related work.

“Deep Asymmetric Multi-task Feature Learning” [a] is indeed significantly different from our work. They define the goal of multi-task feature learning as “…jointly train models for all T tasks simultaneously…”. By this definition, we are not performing multi-task feature learning. Rather, we are attempting to learn knowledge embeddings from a set of networks that were independently pretrained on a set of different tasks T. This difference is subtle but important because multi-task feature learning creates feedback between the learning of all tasks, feedback which is absent in our system. Also, our approach does not assume access to the datasets/tasks that were used to train the individual task networks (i.e. source/teacher networks). Additionally, their use of autoencoder differs from ours. They use the autoencoder as a regularizer to denoise their latent features rather than reconstruct the samples to the input space X.

“Variational Information Distillation for Knowledge Transfer” [1] seeks perform distillation, while MIKE does not. Note the following excerpt from our paper: “It should be clarified that MIKE does not perform true distillation, since our target network (equivalently student network) does not explicitly learn to perform the task of the source network(s) (equivalently teacher network(s)).”

> The choice of the architecture for the auto-encoder is not clear. How are the number of layers for encoder/decoder chosen?

Our approach allows the use of a wide range of different autoencoder architectures. For our preliminary experiments, we chose to mimic EfficientNet simply because it is well tested in the literature and results in a relatively small model size.

> Also, if the reconstruction is nearly perfect owing to the number of parameters in auto-encoder, how does this impact the learning (gradients/parameter updates) of the auto-encoder network and the shared embedding space?

The reconstructions produced were nowhere near perfect, likely due to a combination of our relatively small training sets and small number of parameters in our auto-encoder. However, if the auto-encoder were of sufficient capacity to memorize the training set or learn a highly accurate mapping through the embedding space, we would expect the resulting embeddings to contain very little generalizable information. In our future experiments, we plan to explore the effects of latent dimensionality and auto-encoder topology on information content of the embeddings.

> The claims of scalability of the approach and the quality of the embeddings learnt by the method is not demonstrated in the experiments… There are issues regarding the training instability when considering deeper source networks. This should be discussed in more detail. This can potentially be resolved with the proper weighting of the loss functions?... Please clarify on what basis or parameters is the choice of the dataset partitioning and the experimental setup made. As of now it seems to be arbitrary. The experiments do not particularly demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach over the existing methods.

Thank you for the suggestions. These are all things we plan to address in our follow-up experiments. In the meantime, we will be withdrawing the submission from ICLR 2022.
